<explanation>
Based on our analysis of the complete file tree and the README, Koel is a full‐stack web application that serves as a personal audio streaming service. It uses Laravel on the backend (organized according to MVC and service‐oriented patterns) and Vue.js for the frontend. Here’s how you can break down and represent the system architecture in a diagram that is both complete and tailored to Koel:

1. Identifying Main Components:
   • Frontend: The client-side application written in Vue.js (located in the “resources/assets/js” directory, along with Vue components, tests, and related configuration files). It manages the user interface, client routing, state management (via “stores”), and consumption of API endpoints.
   • Backend API & Web Server: The Laravel application (directories such as “app”, “config”, “routes”, “database”, and “resources/views”). This layer handles HTTP requests, business logic (controllers, services, repositories), authentication (including API endpoints under “app/Http/Controllers/API”), and rendering views (Blade templates).
   • Database: MySQL/PostgreSQL (based on migration files in “database/migrations”) that supports user data, songs, playlists, interactions, and other media-related information.
   • External Integrations and Services: 
       – Several integrations with third-party music and media APIs (e.g., Lastfm, Spotify, YouTube, iTunes, LemonSqueezy for licensing, and others) handled by dedicated classes in “app/Http/Integrations” and “app/Services”.
       – File storage services such as local storage, Dropbox, S3-compatible storage (found under “app/Filesystems”, “app/Services/SongStorages”, etc.).
       – Streaming components located in “app/Services/Streamer” to manage audio streaming.
   • Additional Tools & Testing: 
       – Cypress and PHP unit tests (shown in “tests/Feature”, “tests/Unit”, and “cypress” directories) to ensure quality and correct operations.
       – CLI commands (in “app/Console/Commands”) allow maintenance tasks such as scanning media files, managing playlists, and handling licenses.

2. Defining Relationships and Data Flow:
   • The Frontend interacts with the Backend mainly through API calls (often RESTful endpoints managed by Laravel controllers under “app/Http/Controllers/API”). Display and client logic are fully managed by Vue components.
   • The Backend sits on top of the Database (engaged via Laravel’s Eloquent ORM found in “app/Models” and corresponding migrations) and uses business logic (in “app/Services”, “app/Repositories”) to process requests. Controllers and middleware (in “app/Http/Middleware”) verify, authenticate, and authorize requests.
   • External integrations are used as both data sources and active services to enrich the media experience (for example, Lastfm feedback, album covers, or playlist collaboration services). These services are communicated with via dedicated connectors and requests.
   • Storage services manage audio files and other media assets, and the application supports multiple storage backends (local, cloud, etc.).

3. Key Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • MVC Pattern: The Laravel backend is structured around MVC with Models, Views (Blade templates), and Controllers handling the API logic.
   • Service-Oriented Architecture: Many functionalities (e.g., license handling, media scanning, playlist management) are encapsulated in services to keep the controllers lean and ensure separation of concerns.
   • Modular and Extensible Design: With directories dedicated to integrations (for Lastfm, Spotify, etc.) and separate repositories, the architecture makes it clear where additional modules or third-party integrations can be plugged in.
   • Testing and Continuous Integration: A rich set of tests (unit, integration, and end-to-end tests in Cypress) illustrate the commitment to quality and enable continuous deployment workflows (as seen in the GitHub workflow configuration).

4. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   • Split the diagram into two primary sections: the Frontend and the Backend.
   • For the Frontend:
         – Represent Vue.js components, the client state (stores), and routing.
         – Indicate how API calls flow from the frontend to the backend endpoints.
   • For the Backend:
         – Diagram the MVC layers (Controllers, Models, Views).
         – Clearly show additional layers like the Service and Repository layers.
         – Illustrate the Database as the persistent storage.
         – Highlight External Integrations (draw connectors from the backend’s integration modules to external services such as Lastfm, Spotify, etc.).
         – Include the File Storage systems (annotating choices such as local, Dropbox, or S3).
   • Use directional arrows to show request flow (e.g., UI initiates API requests to controllers, which then query models and call services, etc.).

5. Instructing the Principal Software Engineer on Diagram Elements:
   • Label each major component clearly (e.g., “Vue.js Frontend”, “Laravel API Controllers”, “Business Services”, “Database”, “External Media APIs”, “Storage Services”).
   • Use directional arrows to indicate data flow – for example, arrows from Frontend → API layer, API layer → Database, API layer → External Integrations, etc.
   • Apply color coding or different shapes to differentiate between types of components:
         – Use one color/shape for client-side components (e.g., rectangles for Vue.js modules).
         – A different color for backend layers (controllers, services) and icons for databases and external services.
   • Add annotations that mention key technologies (e.g., “Laravel (PHP Framework)”, “Vue.js (JavaScript Framework)”, “Eloquent ORM”, “RESTful API”, “GitHub Actions for CI/CD”) to provide context.

6. Emphasize Detail and Clarity:
   • Ensure each component and its relationships are captured, even if it means breaking down some areas into subcomponents (such as the detailed structure within the “app/Services” or “app/Http/Controllers/API” directories).
   • Do not shy away from complexity; the goal is to map out as many components and interactions as possible to provide a full picture of how Koel’s architecture is set up.

By following these instructions, your system design diagram will effectively depict Koel’s layered, modular architecture from the user interface down to the database and external integrations. The diagram will help anyone reviewing it to understand the flow of data, how different parts are interconnected, and where key technologies and architectural patterns come into play.
</explanation>
